title: Shawnee Chillicothe divisions
summary: Chillicothe was the Shawnee division that supplied political leadership; its main town moved often in Ohio, so several “Chillicothes” appear in the record.
bodyMarkdown:
The Shawnee were not a single town or a single band. Written sources describe five divisions, each with its own name and traditional duties. One of them, the Chalahgawtha, gave its name to a string of towns called Chillicothe, several of which shaped the history of Kentucky.

## Five divisions

The [Wikipedia article on the Chalahgawtha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chalahgawtha) lists the five as the Chalahgawtha (Chillicothe), Mekoche, Kispoko, Pekowi and Hathawekela. Together they formed the loose confederacy that made up the Shawnee people. By tradition each division served the whole tribe in certain ways, and the Chalahgawtha provided political leadership. The article adds that these customs were already fading when European Americans first wrote them down in the 1700s.

Sources disagree on how kinship worked within the divisions. The [Grokipedia entry on the Shawnee](https://grokipedia.com/page/Shawnee) describes the clans as patrilineal in its section on social structure. Its opening summary calls them matrilineal clans. Grokipedia also says the Mekoche tended to supply ceremonial authority, and that war leaders were chosen for proven skill rather than birth alone.

## A town that moved

The division chief's home village was called Chillicothe, and when the people relocated, the new village took the name too. Not every resident belonged to the Chalahgawtha division, and people from other nations lived there as well. The result is many Chillicothes in the record, a source of confusion for researchers.

Scholars think the Shawnee name of [Lower Shawneetown](/stories/lower-shawneetown-at-the-scioto-mouth/), founded about 1734 at the Scioto mouth, may have been Chillicothe. After it was abandoned in 1758, a Chillicothe on the Scioto near Paint Creek (1758–1787) was one of seven Shawnee villages on the Scioto. In 1762 it held about 300 warriors, perhaps 1,200 people in all.

## Old Chillicothe and Kentucky

During the Revolution, many residents moved to Old Chillicothe on the Little Miami River (1774–1780). It was the home of the war chief [Blackfish](/stories/blackfish-cot-ta-wa-ma-go-chillicothe-war-chief/). From there, Shawnee warriors raided Kentucky, aiming to drive out settlers from their hunting grounds. Daniel Boone was captured in 1778, brought to Chillicothe and adopted into the tribe.

Kentuckians struck back. Americans attacked the town on May 29, 1779, in [John Bowman's raid](/stories/col-john-bowman-at-old-chillicothe/). Blackfish defended it but died later from an infected leg wound.

In 1780, after Bird's invasion of Kentucky, [George Rogers Clark](/stories/george-rogers-clark/) led militia up the Little Miami. The residents left as he approached. Accounts differ on the burning: Clark's men burned the town by one account, while others say the Shawnee burned it themselves to deny plunder to the militia.

The people rebuilt on the Great Miami River (1780–1782). After the Kentucky defeat at Blue Licks, Clark destroyed that Chillicothe and four other villages in November 1782.

## Kentucky today

Kentucky has no Shawnee Chillicothe of its own. Its people meet this history at places such as Lower Shawneetown's Kentucky side and the Blue Licks battlefield, where the towns' wars reached south of the Ohio.
